cards.explanation: The answer is that he prays to the LORD. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), spreads out his hands and speaks straight to God. His words start with “O LORD, God of Israel…” and in verse 28 he calls what he's doing a prayer. Hands up, whole crowd watching, and he talks to God like nobody else is in the room. That's a man who knows who he's talking to.

The answer is those who walk before Him with all their hearts. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), says God keeps His covenant of loving devotion with “…Your servants who walk before You with all their hearts.” The word is ALL, and it's about their hearts. I once put about forty percent of my heart into a batch, and the cookies knew.

The answer is False. Solomon, Israel's king, says God has already kept His promise. He tells God, “You have kept Your promise to Your servant, my father David.” David was Israel's king before Solomon (1 Kings 2:11). Solomon adds that what God spoke with His mouth, He fulfilled with His hand this day. Nobody is waiting on that one, friends.

The answer is that David would never fail to have a man on the throne. Solomon quotes God telling David, “You will never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel…” David was Israel's king before Solomon (1 Kings 2:11). The promise is about a man always being on that throne, and it has a condition attached, which comes right up.

The answer is True. Solomon quotes the whole thing: “…if only your descendants guard their way to walk before Me as you have done.” David was Israel's king before him (1 Kings 2:11), and the throne promise was spoken to David. So there's an “if only” in the middle of it. Listen for those little words, friends, they carry weight.

The answer is that the temple can't contain God, and neither can heaven. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), says it plainly: “The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built.” He's talking about a temple he says he built, and he still says it. I can't even fit my hat through the oven door, and he's talking about God not fitting in the highest heavens. Humbling stuff.

The answer is so He'll hear prayers prayed toward the temple. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), asks God to keep His eyes open toward it “so that You may hear the prayer that Your servant prays toward this place.” It's about God hearing prayers. Open eyes, open ears, night and day. That's a lot of attention, friends.

The answer is “heaven.” Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), says, “May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place.” Prayers go toward the temple, but he places God's dwelling in heaven. That fits what he just said, that even the highest heavens can't contain God (verse 27).

The answer is True. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), asks for both in one breath: “May You hear and forgive.” Hear their plea, and then forgive. You'll notice that second part keeps coming back through the whole prayer.

The answer is to condemn the wicked and justify the righteous. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), asks God to act and to judge. He asks for “…condemning the wicked man by bringing down on his own head what he has done, and justifying the righteous man by rewarding him according to his righteousness.” He's asking God to sort it out from heaven.

The answer is returning to God and praying in the temple. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), imagines the people defeated because of sin, and then “…they return to You and confess Your name, praying and pleading with You in this temple…” Their return is to God, and then Solomon asks God to hear and forgive.

The answer is False. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), doesn't ask for a new land. He asks God to “…forgive the sin of Your people Israel.” and to “…restore them to the land You gave to their fathers.” The same land, given back.

The answers are “confess” and “turn.” Verse 35 says the people “…pray toward this place and confess Your name…” Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), pictures them confessing God's name when the rain is gone. He also says they “…turn from their sins because You have afflicted them…” They confess God's name, and they turn from their sins.

The answer is to teach them the good way to walk. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), asks God to forgive “…so that You may teach them the good way in which they should walk.” Then he asks for rain too. So there's a teacher in this prayer, and it's God.

The answer is according to all his ways. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), asks God to “…repay each man according to all his ways, since You know his heart…” And he adds that God alone knows the hearts of all men. That's not a job for a stamper.

The answer is True. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), says it right there: “…for You alone know the hearts of all men…” That's why he asks God to repay each man according to his ways, since God knows his heart. No one else can see all the way in.

The answer is to do all the foreigner asks Him. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), asks God to “…hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You.” That's a wide open door. He's asking that someone from a distant land who prays toward the temple be heard too.

The answer is that all peoples will know God's name. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), says, “Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel…” He also says they will know this house is called by God's Name. That's the result he pictures when God answers the foreigner.

The answer is to hear them and uphold their cause. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), asks, “…then may You hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and may You uphold their cause.” The people are out at war, praying toward the city God chose. He asks for God's ear and God's backing.

The answer is that an enemy takes them captive to his land. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), says God becomes angry and delivers them “…to an enemy who takes them as captives to his own land, whether far or near…” It's a heavy part of the prayer. And he follows it right away with a way back.

The answer is True. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), pictures that very thing. In verse 47 they “…come to their senses in the land to which they were taken, and they repent and plead with You in the land of their captors…” They say they have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly. Honest words, in a hard place.

The answer is with all their heart and soul. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), says they “…return to You with all their heart and soul in the land of the enemies who took them captive…” All their heart and soul, even there. That's a full return, with nothing held back.

The answer is “compassion.” Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), asks God to “…grant them compassion in the eyes of their captors to show them mercy.” He's asking God to soften the hearts of the people holding them. That's a prayer for mercy from the captors.

The answer is that they're His people and His inheritance. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), gives this reason: “For they are Your people and Your inheritance…” He reminds God of who they belong to. Then he adds that God brought them out of Egypt.

The answer is False. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), prays, “May Your eyes be open to the pleas of Your servant and of Your people Israel, and may You listen to them whenever they call to You.” That's whenever, not only inside one building. He even pictures captives praying toward the city and the house from an enemy's land.

The answer is Moses. Solomon, Israel's king (1 Kings 4:1), says God set Israel apart “…as You spoke through Your servant Moses when You brought our fathers out of Egypt.” Moses was Israel's leader (Psalm 77:20). The prayer ends by pointing back to that old word.
